title: Design a Chess Game — Object Model
prompt: Design the object model for a two-player chess game. Model the board, the pieces with their distinct movement rules, move validation (including special moves like castling, en passant, and promotion), check/checkmate/stalemate detection, and the overall game state. Design the core classes and key methods. Focus on the object design, not a chess AI. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: Per-piece movement via Strategy/polymorphism, special-move rules, and check/checkmate detection with a clean game state machine.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Separates functional (legal moves per piece, special moves, check/mate/stalemate, turns) from non-functional (rule correctness, extensibility to variants, undo).

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Board, Cell/Square, Piece (+ subtypes), Move, Player, Game, MoveValidator — cleanly separated, no god class.

rubric.label: Class design & responsibilities
rubric.description: Piece movement is polymorphic/Strategy, not a switch on type; Board holds state; Game orchestrates turns and end conditions.

rubric.label: Relationships & cardinality
rubric.description: Board composes 64 Cells; Cell holds 0..1 Piece; Piece has a color/owner; Game has two Players and a Board and move history.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: Strategy/polymorphism for movement, Factory for piece creation/promotion, State for game phase, Command/Memento for move + undo, Singleton for board optional.

rubric.label: SOLID / OCP
rubric.description: Adding a variant piece or rule requires new classes, not editing existing pieces; validation composed, not a monolith.

rubric.label: API / method design
rubric.description: getValidMoves(piece), makeMove(move), isCheck/isCheckmate/isStalemate, promote, undo — clear signatures.

rubric.label: Game state & rules engine
rubric.description: Turn alternation, game phases (active/check/checkmate/stalemate/draw), and legal-move filtering that respects check.

rubric.label: Edge cases / special moves
rubric.description: Castling (rights, path, not through check), en passant, promotion, pinned pieces, self-check prevention, draw conditions.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: Chess variants (Chess960, custom pieces), undo/redo, move notation, network/AI players added cleanly.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Narrates the class diagram and move-validation flow, states tradeoffs, reasons about check filtering.

functional_requirements: Represent an 8x8 board with pieces placed in the standard initial position
Generate/validate legal moves per piece type (pawn, knight, bishop, rook, queen, king)
Support special moves: castling, en passant, pawn promotion
Detect check, checkmate, stalemate, and common draws
Alternate turns between two players; maintain move history
Reject illegal moves (blocked path, wrong turn, leaving own king in check)
nonfunctional_requirements: Rule correctness — the crux; especially self-check prevention and special moves
Extensible to variants and new piece types without editing existing pieces (OCP)
Clean separation of board state, movement rules, and game orchestration
clarifying_questions: Standard chess only, or must the model support variants (Chess960, custom pieces)?
Do we need move generation (all legal moves) or just validation of a proposed move?
Are players human-only, or should the model allow an AI/network player?
Do we auto-detect draws (threefold repetition, 50-move, insufficient material)?

core_classes.name: Board
core_classes.responsibility: Holds the 8x8 grid of Cells and provides piece placement/lookup and path queries.

core_classes.name: Cell / Square
core_classes.responsibility: One square; holds 0..1 Piece and its coordinates.

core_classes.name: Piece (abstract)
core_classes.responsibility: Base for all pieces; defines movement contract polymorphically.

core_classes.name: Pawn / Knight / Bishop / Rook / Queen / King
core_classes.responsibility: Concrete movement rules; Pawn handles double-step/en-passant/promotion, King handles castling/one-square, sliders handle path.

core_classes.name: Move
core_classes.responsibility: Command object: a reversible move with metadata for special moves and undo.

core_classes.name: MoveValidator / RulesEngine
core_classes.responsibility: Filters piece candidate moves to fully legal ones — path clear, turn, and does-not-leave-own-king-in-check.

core_classes.name: Player
core_classes.responsibility: A participant with a color; may be human/AI/network.

core_classes.name: Game
core_classes.responsibility: Orchestrates turns, applies moves via the validator, tracks state, detects end conditions.

core_classes.name: PieceFactory
core_classes.responsibility: Creates pieces for setup and promotion.

core_classes.name: GameState (enum/state)
core_classes.responsibility: ACTIVE, CHECK, CHECKMATE, STALEMATE, DRAW, RESIGNED.

relationships: Board composes 64 Cells; each Cell holds 0..1 Piece (composition/aggregation).
Piece is abstract; each concrete piece overrides its movement — polymorphism replaces a type switch.
Move is a Command referencing moved/captured pieces and enough info to undo (Memento-ish).
Game composes a Board, two Players, a move History, and a GameState; delegates legality to MoveValidator.
MoveValidator depends only on Board + Piece abstractions (it asks pieces for candidate moves, then filters).

design_patterns.where: Each Piece subclass encapsulates its own movement rule
design_patterns.why: Movement varies per piece; new pieces are added as subclasses without touching a central switch (OCP).

design_patterns.where: PieceFactory for initial setup and pawn promotion
design_patterns.why: Centralizes piece construction; promotion swaps a pawn for a chosen piece cleanly.

design_patterns.where: Move.execute/undo capturing captured piece and prior state
design_patterns.why: Enables undo/redo and 'try move, check for self-check, revert' without duplicating board state.
Game phase governs what actions are legal and drives end detection.

apis: game.makeMove(from, to) -> MoveResult (accepts or rejects with reason)
state_transitions: Turn: WHITE_TO_MOVE ↔ BLACK_TO_MOVE after each legal move
Game: ACTIVE → CHECK (king attacked) → back to ACTIVE (escaped) | CHECKMATE (no legal move & in check)
ACTIVE → STALEMATE (no legal move & not in check) | DRAW (repetition/50-move/insufficient material) | RESIGNED
Legal-move generation = pseudo-legal candidates filtered by 'does not leave own king in check'
edge_cases: Self-check: a move that exposes your own king is illegal even if geometrically valid (pinned piece)
Castling: king & rook unmoved, no pieces between, king not currently in check and doesn't pass through or land on an attacked square
En passant: only immediately after the opponent's two-square pawn advance
Promotion: pawn reaching the last rank must promote (choose piece)
Checkmate vs stalemate: both have no legal moves; differ by whether the king is in check
Draws: threefold repetition, fifty-move rule, insufficient material
Attempting to move on the wrong turn, or capturing your own piece
concurrency: Turn-based, so no in-game data race in the classic sense — enforce single-writer per turn
For a server hosting many games: one lock/actor per Game; moves serialized per game
Move validation uses try-move-then-undo — must be atomic within a turn (no concurrent mutation of that board)
Immutable Move records + explicit undo keep state transitions reasoning-friendly
extensibility: New piece type / variant piece → new Piece subclass, register in PieceFactory, no edits to others
Chess960 → different initial setup via the factory; movement unchanged
Undo/redo & PGN notation → derive from the Move history
AI or network player → a Player implementation; Game is agnostic
Draw-detection rules → pluggable rule objects consulted by the RulesEngine

deep_dives.probe: How does a bishop's move differ from a knight's in your model? Show me why adding a new fairy piece doesn't require editing any existing piece or a central switch.
A knight is pinned to its king. Its normal L-move is geometrically legal but would expose the king. Where and how do you reject that? Walk through the try-move/undo check.
Model castling. What state must you track (has the king/rook moved, is the king passing through check), and where does that logic live — King, Move, or validator?
How do you distinguish checkmate from stalemate? Describe the algorithm using legal-move generation.
How do you implement undo cleanly, including undoing a capture, en passant, and promotion?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions piece or move rule or switch
followup_bank.question: Is movement a switch on piece type or polymorphic per subclass? Add a custom 'archbishop' piece — what changes?
A pinned piece's move is geometrically legal but exposes the king. Where do you reject it, and how?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions castle or castling or en passant or promotion
followup_bank.question: Where does the special-move logic and its required state (hasMoved, last double-step) live? Defend that placement.
Both have zero legal moves. What's the exact condition that separates them, and how do you compute legal moves?
How do you undo a move that was a capture-plus-promotion? What does the Move need to store?

tradeoffs: Polymorphic piece movement (OCP, more classes) vs a central move table (compact, harder to extend)
Generate all legal moves (clean mate detection, costlier) vs validate on demand (cheap, mate detection harder)
Try-move/undo for self-check (simple, correct) vs incremental attack maps (fast, complex)
Move as Command with undo (enables history/redo) vs plain from/to (simpler, no undo)
reference.reference_answer: A strong senior answer makes movement polymorphic — each Piece subclass encapsulates its own rule so a new piece is a new class (OCP), never a switch. Board holds the grid; Move is a Command carrying enough state (captured piece, type, promotion) to execute and undo; and a MoveValidator generates pseudo-legal candidate moves from pieces then filters out any that leave the mover's own king in check — the try-move/undo pattern that also handles pins. It places special-move state where it belongs (hasMoved for castling, last double-step for en passant), distinguishes checkmate from stalemate via legal-move generation plus check status, and models the game as a state machine. Senior signal: the self-check filtering algorithm and clean special-move handling without polluting every class.

interviewer_notes: The senior differentiators are (1) polymorphic movement instead of a switch — probe with 'add a custom piece'; and (2) correct self-check / pin handling via generate-then-filter (try-move/undo), which trips up most candidates. Make them show exactly where a pinned piece's move is rejected. Push on one special move in depth (castling is richest — rights, path, not-through-check). Ensure checkmate vs stalemate is computed from legal-move generation, not hacked. Move-as-Command with undo is strong signal. Don't let them build a chess AI — this is object design. Time-box entity setup so the rules engine gets the spotlight.
